about: Data for the Food Garden Planner pictures (static/garden/viz). Weeks are counted from the gardener's own average last spring frost date.

fields.ht: Height rank used to place crops on the garden map: 4 tree, 3 tall or trellised, 2 medium, 1 low. Texas A&M E-289 names okra, corn and tomatoes as tall crops to group on the north side; VCE 426-312 says to put tall and trellised crops on the north side. Oregon State's raised-bed handout puts pole beans, trellised peas and tomatoes on the north side of an east-west bed and says a north-south bed is best for low crops. The ranks for the other crops follow typical plant size (editorial).
fields.pw: Planting window in weeks from the average last spring frost (negative = before), from the CSU planting groups: hardy as early as 2 to 4 weeks before; semi-hardy 0 to 2 weeks before; tender, from seed, around the frost date (drawn as 1 week either side); very tender 2 or more weeks after (drawn as 2 to 4 weeks, fading out). Crops a source says to plant after the frost date (WSU dry beans, WVU sunflowers, USU peanuts) are drawn 0 to 2 weeks after. The planner's crop notes (ps) give the source for each crop.
fields.si: Age of transplants when set out, in weeks (CSU Table 1 and 2): tomato 5 to 7, pepper 6 to 8, eggplant 6 to 9, broccoli and cabbage 5 to 7.
fields.hv: pick: picked again and again once the first fruit or leaves are ready (Iowa State harvest guide: tomatoes weekly, cucumbers and summer squash every 2 to 3 days), drawn until the average first fall frost, which kills frost-tender crops (UNL G1343, CSU). once: harvested when mature; the window spans the planner's days-to-harvest range, from early to late varieties.
fields.fall: A second crop can be sown for fall. Latest sowing = first fall frost minus days to harvest minus the 14-day Fall Factor, minus 14 more days for frost-tender crops (UNL G1343). The window runs from late varieties to early ones. The UNL count also adds the length of the harvest you want, so sow earlier for a longer harvest.
fields.fd: Cowpeas: about 65 to 75 days before the average first fall frost (University of Arkansas, in the planner's crop data).

sun.text: Most vegetables need at least 6 hours of direct sun a day (Texas A&M E-289); 8 to 10 hours is ideal, and fruit and seed crops do best with at least 8 (VCE 426-312). Leafy greens and some herbs get by with less (the planner's crop data, from Iowa State).

bed.text: Make beds at most 4 feet wide if you can reach in from both sides, so you never step on the soil; walkways 14 to 16 inches wide work between raised beds (Oregon State). Paths of 3 to 4 feet fit a wheelbarrow or a wheelchair (the planner's Large home gardens guide).

garlic.note: Plant cloves in fall; harvest the next summer when the leaves turn brown.

fava_beans.note: Sown in fall for a spring crop where winters are mild; timing for cold-winter areas wasn't verified.

microgreens.note: Grown indoors year-round, ready in 1 to 3 weeks.

culinary_herbs.note: Timing depends on the herb: basil is frost-tender, parsley and cilantro like cool weather.

strawberries.note: Planted once, in early spring; most fruit comes from the second year on.

blueberries.note: Planted once, in early spring; full crops from about year 3 or 4.

raspberries_blackberries.note: Planted once, in early spring; fruit from about the second year.

grapes.note: Planted once, in early spring, on a trellis; fruit from about year 3.

rhubarb.note: Planted once as crowns in early spring; light picking from year 2 or 3.

asparagus.note: Planted once as crowns in early spring; first spears in year 2 or 3.

jerusalem_artichokes.note: Planted once, early in spring; it spreads and comes back every year.

apple.note: Planted once, as a young tree; see “Ready in” for the years to first fruit.
